subject: Dead Sea
note: Cited to a pinned Wikipedia revision (trusted_secondary): Dead Sea (revision 1384259663). Figures are quoted as the page states them. The page gives no outline of the 1930 lake, so none is drawn: the map shows today's lake with figures and captions only. The lake is the only named place; no country is highlighted, labelled or named in the narration beyond what the page says about the Jordan River's diversion, and the frames stay on the water. The page's own area figures (1,050 km² in 1930, 605 km² 'today') carry no year for 'today', so the script says 'today'.

claims.text: The Dead Sea is a landlocked salt lake bordered by Jordan to the east, the West Bank to the west and Israel to the southwest; its main tributary is the Jordan River.
As of 2025, the lake's surface is 439.78 metres below sea level, making its shores the lowest land-based elevation on Earth.
The Dead Sea is receding at a swift rate; its surface area today is 605 km², having been 1,050 km² in 1930.

From a water surface of 395 m below sea level in 1970 it fell 22 m to 418 m below sea level in 2006, reaching a drop rate of 1 m per year; by 2025 it reached 439 m below sea level, a drop of more than 1 m per year.
The Dead Sea has been rapidly shrinking since the 1960s because of diversion of incoming water from the Jordan River to the north as part of the National Water Carrier scheme, completed in 1964.

The annual flow into the Dead Sea from the Jordan is, as of 2021, less than 100,000,000 cubic metres (100 million), compared with former flows of between 1,200,000,000 and 1,300,000,000 cubic metres (1.2 to 1.3 billion).
As of 2021, the surface of the Sea has shrunk by about 33 percent since the 1960s.
The Dead Sea level drop is believed to be the cause of the recent appearance of large sinkholes along the western shore, where most beach resorts of the northern basin had to be shut down.
